text: The assembly will hear an address by her
excellency Mia Amour Mle, Prime
Minister, Minister for Economic Affairs
and Development and Minister for
National Security of Barbados. I request
protocol to escort her excellency and
invite her to address the assembly.
Mr. President, excellencies, my friends,
we meet at a time when the obstacles
confronting human progress are
multiplying.
Obstacles to peace, obstacles to food
and clean water, obstacles to finance,
medicine and education,
obstacles to movement and opportunity,
obstacles to technology, to the
knowledge and infrastructure needed to
use it. and increasingly obstacles
between nations, between communities,
and between people who no longer agree
on the same facts or trust the same
institutions.
War continues to destroy lives and
communities. Even though the
international community possesses more
tools than ever, ever before to prevent
conflict and to facilitate dialogue, the
climate crisis is accelerating.
Even though the science is clear enough
for us to act and many of the solutions
are already known and despite
unprecedented global wealth, millions
remain without reliable access to food,
water, health or shelter.
These challenges, my friends, are
creating the poly crises of which we
constantly speak. And at the same time,
new challenges are emerging.
Artificial intelligence is opening
extraordinary possibilities in health,
education, science, and productivity
while also creating new risk of
exclusion, exploitation, surveillance,
and the distortion of truth. And yet,
the cooperation needed to confront these
challenges
under strain. It is why I believe the
theme this year is so apt. Restoring
trust, managing transformation, a united
nation that delivers for all. The theme
reminds us that we have institutions
created to preserve peace, to advance
development, and yes, to protect human
dignity. The institutions are these very
United Nations.
We have shared principles grounded in
sovereign equality and in the
recognition that our responsibilities
extend beyond borders. The reality is
that we understand
that there is regrettably
enough for us to be able to invest in
prevention rather than waiting to
finance reconstruction.
We understand enough about the climate
crisis to reduce the emissions that are
warming our planet and take the
necessary steps for our populations
to adapt.
We equally now understand enough about
the rapid development of AI to know that
as we welcome its promise, we must
anchor its development in a universal
humanizing
framework that does not imperil our
existence as human beings. The failure,
my friends, to address these challenges,
therefore, is not one simply of
knowledge or capacity. It is our
repeated failure to convert what we know
into what we do. To turn principle into
practice and global capacity into
solidarity.
So beneath our many crises lies yet
another one. And yes, it is a crisis of
responsibility.
Mr. President, that responsibility
begins here in these halls. The
transformation we seek for a better
world will only happen when we trust
each other and we accept our
responsibility for each other. We in the
Caribbean understand something about the
necessity of living together. We had no
choice.
Barbadian novelist and essaist George
Laming once described the Caribbean as
perhaps the first global experiment in
human history bringing together and I
quote every branch of the human family
from the indigenous peoples of the
Americas to the diverse peoples from
Africa, Europe and Asia. It is as though
that we through this torturous and
shared history of migration, conquest,
slavery, and the difficult work of
constructing a common national and
regional destiny that we give the world
an example to follow. Against all the
odds, the Caribbean produced what Laming
called a new kind of global family.
Our history has taught us that
difference need not mean division, that
coexistence requires dialogue and
negotiation,
and that those without the power to
compel must learn the power of
persuasion.
These are not merely Caribbean lessons.
They're universal.
And it is in this spirit I'd like to
thank her excellency Annalena Burbach
for her leadership of the general
assembly's 80th session and for helping
to advance the work of the member states
on UN reform
and to you Mr. President. Barbados
extends its warm congratulations.
We look forward to your stewardship of
this assembly and we move to restore
trust and indeed to carry reforms from
proposals to implementation.
But reform cannot be selective. We
cannot move swiftly to reorganize
offices and reporting lines while
allowing the most consequential
questions of power and representation to
remain unresolved.
transformation and development,
peacekeeping and humanitarian aid cannot
succeed if member states are unwilling
to fund it. Let's be very clear, no
organizational chart can overcome the
refusal of states to respect decisions
that they find inconvenient.
We cannot continue to ask international
organizations to do more while failing
to provide them with the resources
necessary to fulfill the mandates that
we ourselves have agreed.
And if member states believe in the
institutions
that they have created, then we must
also be prepared to sustain them.
Barbados has consistently met that
responsibility
and I give this body the assurance that
we will continue to do so. Our
commitment to multilateralism, to an
international rules-based order must be
measured not only by what we ask of
these institutions but by our
willingness to support them. So yes, let
us improve the machinery but let us also
reform the exercise of power. The
Security Council still has 15 members,
five of them permanent and armed with
that veto.
Africa with 54 states has no permanent
seat. And you've heard speaker after
speaker after speaker come to this
platform to say that this must change.
Small island developing states equally
confront threats that now reach squarely
into the council's mandate from climate
insecurity and illicit arm flows to
organized crime and displacement. And
yet despite constituting one quarter of
the world states we have no assured
representation within the councils. This
too my friends must change
and the world we know has already
changed. The council has not changed
with it.
But reform is not only about who sits at
the table. It is about how power is
exercised.
Barbados is therefore joining 123 other
member states in supporting the Franco
Mexican initiative on the use of the
veto in the cases of mass atrocities.
Its principle is fundamental.
where populations face genocide,
crimes against humanity or large-scale
war crimes, the veto should not be
allowed to paralyze the Security Council
when action is most urgently needed.
This is why people are losing trust in
the United Nations and its council. And
Mr. President, it's not fair to the
majority of member states who still
believe in the promise of this body.
Even as we call for greater equity with
the reform of the security council,
we must equally reform the secretariat
to better support peacekeeping and the
resolution of conflicts. We've been told
that there are more conflicts today than
at any time since the United Nations was
established. And regrettably, these
conflicts are in almost every corner of
the planet. The Oslo Peace Institute
reported that in 2025, last year,
individuals faced battle related deaths.
That is almost Barbadis' population.
I'm told that this makes it the third
most violent year in the postcold war
era. My friends, the scale of human
tragedy is mounting. And whether it is
in Gaza or the West Bank or Lebanon or
Yemen or Sudan or Ukraine or elsewhere,
last year we feared
that there was a risk of conflicts in
the Middle East widening even further
and the conflicts continue. These fears
regrettably have come to pass and with a
global impact.
Nevertheless,
indeed, conflicts are more protracted
and more fragmented. And when coupled
with hunger and unsustainable debt on a
warming planet, it becomes a veritable
hell for the citizens of those
countries.
Increases in energy and transport costs
and in interest rates have spurred
inflation. It means that no one even on
the other side of the world can escape
the hardships in meeting their daily
needs. The truth is, until there is a
two-state solution that respects the
rights and territories of both the
Israelis and Palestinians, we will
continue to live on the edge in this
world.
And you may well ask, how have we gotten
here? We need to address with laser-like
focus each and every one of these
conflicts.
Legitimacy demands that of us. And let
us let the UN deliberately and
systematically deploy nimble mediation
teams led by political leaders, current
and retired, on behalf of the Secretary
General and enjoying the Secretary
General's confidence and authority and
the respect of member states. This, my
friends, will help lift the heavy weight
necessary to end these multiple
conflicts and to bring peace and dignity
to those affected populations.
We know that many hands make light work
and we can't ignore it. These conflicts
need to be supported by a quicker and
technology enhanced observer force
capable of rapid deployment to monitor
and support ceasefires and peace
agreements to be given the resources.
These peacekeeping forces must be given
realistic mandates, predictable
financing and true partnership.
Let us work, my friends, together with
the parties to these conflicts to build
dialogue and to bring opportunities for
investment and jobs to the affected
populations so that they too can live
properly. And as for the wider
international legal order, we know that
countries of every size and capacity
depend on a system in which rules are
made collectively and applied
consistently and fairly. But if we don't
act early enough, we have trouble. And
that is why we say that the UN must
receive the resources and the resolve to
act before the guns speak and not after
the guns start to fly. My friends,
without an equitable rules-based order,
smaller states like mine will simply
cease to exist in this world. And that
is why Barbados is a co-sponsor of the
P4M, a group focused on strengthening
multilateralism and to beat back the
undertakers who are waiting to bury it.
Mr. President, I would like to express
profound appreciation to the Secretary
General, my brother Antonio Gutirez.
His voice
has been constant,
steady, and absolutely right on all of
the critical issues facing humanity.
And to his deputy, Amina Muhammad, we
also say thank you for taking the
journey without diverting from the
principles and the core values of this
charter.
As the United Nations undertakes the
important task of selecting its next
secretary general, Barbados joins its
sister member states in the Caribbean
community in pledging its full support
for the candidature of Ambassador
Carolyn Rodriguez Burkett of Guyana
at a moment when the international
community is being called upon to renew
its faith in multilateralism.
We believe that Ambassador Rodriguez
Burkett brings to this task the
experience, the skills and the
understanding to serve the entire
membership of this organization. Indeed,
Mr. President, I believe that others
think so too.
I'd like sir to turn to the topic of
artificial intelligence which is one of
our new challenges. AI is already
transforming how we work, learn and
govern. And it is clear that its
potential is extraordinary. We have
found that it has great capacity to
detect disease earlier, predict
disasters, improve agriculture, and
expand access to education and public
services. And yet these same
extraordinary systems can just as
quickly reproduce discrimination, widen
surveillance, and spread falsehoods
faster than institutions can respond. We
must not allow a new technological age
to reproduce all hierarchies of access
and power. And this is why Barbados is
so honored to host the second in-person
meeting of the Independent International
Scientific Panel on Artificial
Intelligence, which will be held in
November of this year. We recognize that
yesterday's Security Council encounter
may well and should speeden the question
of how we as a global community deals
with this issue. In the growing age of
AI, governance cannot be left to
voluntary corporate practices or to a
small number of technologically advanced
states. We need globally agreed rules
that protect human dignity, preserve
meaningful human oversight, and ensure
that the benefits of AI are shared
widely and equitably.
I caution a technology that will affect
every state must be governed by the
rules that every state has had the
opportunity to shape. Mr. President,
exactly 65 years ago, that great
Caribbean French African intellectual
and psychiatrist France Fallon published
what has now become a classic, The
Wretched of the Earth. And across the
vast range of observations and analysis
that he made in that extraordinarily
lucid and precient book book, he said
the following. What matters today is the
issue which blocks the horizon is the
need for a redistribution of wealth.
Humanity will have to address this
question no matter how devastating the
consequences may be.
My friends, this was haringly true in
and sadly remains manifest today. This
is why Barbados throws its full support
behind the establishment of the
International Panel on inequality that
is being proposed. Growing inequality is
at the center of geopolitical
discussions, tensions, distrust in
institutions, and indeed the increasing
number of conflicts that we see. It is
for this reason that we reject the
notion that governments must refrain
from policy interventions that are
essential to creating a level and fair
playing field for ordinary citizens. We
know that it is the policy choices of
government that has led to this
injustice and it is the policy choices
of governments that must now remove it.
For us, this is as important a battle of
the cl as the climate crisis. And Mr.
President, that brings me to that
crisis.
Minister Murat Kurum representing the
incoming COP 31 presidency has put the
challenge plainly. The time for simply
setting out goals is behind us.
Anyone who experienced this summer in
Europe and elsewhere knows that it was
the hottest on record. And the Super El
Nino has not even yet hit.
The proposed action agenda places
methane reduction at the center of
climate implementation and we welcome
that focus. It is true that carbon
dioxide must remain central to the
global energy transition, but emissions
are not falling quickly enough
and the full benefits of action will
take time to emerge. So, Mr. President
under Barbados's presidency of the CVF
climate vulnerable forum and its V20
countries
74 countries
got together and advanced the call to
pull the methane emergency break. At the
V20 ministerial dialogue in April of
this year, the finance ministers agreed
that methane reduction must be treated
not only as an environmental priority
but also an economic, fiscal, and public
health opportunity.
We must now implement
the climate vulnerable countries need to
mobilize approximately $490
billion each year by 2030. And yet the
current inflows are roughly $90 billion.
As the young people in Barbados would
say, the math simply ain't math.
We must also correct the inequity of the
borrowing cost that these countries
face. It is almost 1.2 two percentage
points higher for climate vulnerable
countries than for advanced economies.
Now, that figure seems small to you, but
that actually generates an estimated $62
billion more a year in excess interest
payments each year. This cannot be fair.
So that believe me when I say that
change is possible as we have seen
consistently with measures from the
Bridgetown initiative. In less than one
year, Barbados as chair of the climate
vulnerable countries, the V20 countries
along with the OPEC fund for
international development designed and
launched the vulnerability to viability
compact on four pillars, bringing about
74 countries along with 16 development
finance institutions globally to expand
access to affordable long-term capital
for education projects, health projects,
and water infrastructure.
The CVF also had its governors of the
central bank meet to establish the
lifeline fund
which will shortly be operationalized.
It seeks to provide rapid liquidity when
climate shocks create balance of
payments pressures for countries. So we
are moving to help ourselves. We have
been resolute and the reason for it is
that we know that you cannot build
hospitals and schools and water
infrastructure with 10 and 15year money.
It crowds out critical investments for
our people and leaves you flatfooted and
that is why this important initiative
represents real progress.
But mechanisms such as this one cannot
on their own address the underlying
flaws of the international financial
architecture.
I repeat that for almost 5 years the
Bridgetown initiative has consistently
argued that climate resilience, debt
sustainability and access to affordable
finance cannot be treated separately.
For many vulnerable countries, the
problem is not simply the availability
of capital, but whether we have the
fiscal space to borrow and to invest on
reasonable terms.
Mr. President, as I turn to my region in
the Caribbean,
I'd like to highlight a series of crises
that continue to threaten our peace,
stability, and development.
Let me say at the outset that when I
speak about letting many hands make
light work when it comes to conflict
resolution that this is one of the areas
in which the political leaders of the
Caribbean can play a pivotal role in its
own region.
Firstly, Haiti. The security crisis
continues to retire political renewal
and economic recovery. And still the
preparations for a return to
constitutional government, yes, are
moving forward even with great
difficulty.
But those efforts cannot succeed
unless security improves,
particularly in the areas containing
more than half of Haiti's electorate in
the capital and surrounding areas.
Barbados therefore supports the full
deployment that has been too too too
long promised and the renewal of the
mandate of the gang suppression force.
Let me remind you that it was in 2022
that this recent more heightened state
of insecurity began with the fuel riots
just before the general assembly met in
And in 2026, we have not kept faith with
providing the level of security that
would minimize the loss of life. At the
same time, we have to give thanks where
thanks is due. And there are member
states who have contributed in whatever
way to helping Haiti find its path. This
includes of course the Caribbean
community's eminent persons group which
has been helping to build consensus and
maintain engagement with key
international partners in the last few
years.
In addition, Mr. President, we are
deeply concerned by the worsening
humanitarian pressures facing the people
of Cuba.
Too many people are suffering. Too many
people. Restrictions on trade, finance,
and access to fuel are intensifying
hardship, not only for Cuban citizens,
but for all others who study and live
there. Barbados has each year opposed
the use of the embargo and other
unilateral coercive measures against
Cuba. And as always, we call for
constructive engagement.
constructive engagement grounded in
dialogue, sovereign equality, and
respect for international law. That is
why we are here as individual states. We
will also extend our continued
solidarity to the people of Venezuela
who regrettably are recovering from the
devastating double earthquakes in June.
The horror was mind-blowing.
Barbados was proud to stand with our
neighbor in the immediate aftermath,
dispatching our field hospital and
personnel to Venezuela. We remain
committed to supporting them in their
longer term recovery. A stable,
sovereign, peaceful, and democratic
Venezuela is vital to the security and
prosperity of not just Latin America,
but the wider Caribbean.
In this regard, however, I must take
this opportunity to reiterate Barbados's
steadfast support to its sister of
Cariccom, its sister Caraccom country,
Guyana, as it seeks to bring a peaceful
resolution through the International
Court of Justice for the long
outstanding territorial controversy with
Venezuela. This is in the interests of
the people of Guyana, the people of
Venezuela, and the wider people of the
Caribbean and Latin America. The
Caribbean, my friends, must remain a
zone of peace. We cannot accept our
region becoming a theater.
We cannot accept our region becoming a
theater for confrontation or for the
unilateral and unjustified use of force.
Mr. President, brings me to another
matter. On March 25th of this year, a
historic resolution was passed in this
general assembly. The overwhelming
majority of states acknowledged the
truth that we in the Caribbean long knew
the trafficking of enslaved African and
racialized cattle enslavement of
Africans
is the gravest crime against humanity.
and we know it. Regrettably, we still
carry the scars.
I've reminded us that it was my country,
Barbados, that passed the first slave
code that the world knew in 1661 to deal
with cattle slavery.
Others regrettably followed, including
the infamous code noir of 1685.
That codeir was only repealed this year
and then hence the wounds are still raw.
We in Barbados accept the moral
responsibility of removing the cross of
slavery with its horrific consequences.
We must effect healing through
reparatory justice for it is the right
thing to do.
As a result, in July of this year,
CARACOM heads of government approved the
revised CARACOM 10-point plan for
reparatory justice for the Caribbean,
for Africa, and for those countries
concerned. The honest engagement must
begin. And I thank President Mahama of
Ghana for coming to the table with the
force with which he has come.
We do not ask for reparations without
accepting responsibility for our own
self-repair which we have undertaken for
decades. I want to be very clear about
this. Mr. Spe, Mr. President, I make the
same mistake as President Muhammad.
We are parliamentarians.
I want to make this clear.
Let there be no doubt, Mr. president
that the mindset that established,
justified, and sustained slavery is the
same mindset that sustains the
iniquities and the inequities within the
power structures of this very
institution and within the international
financial architecture. It is the same
mindset.
It is the same mindset that caused a
global map to remain grossly inaccurate
on the size of Africa for centuries.
As if the true size of Africa would
intimidate the rest of the world into
understanding its power. Mr. President,
if we want to restore trust in these
United Nations and we want to manage
transformation as is your theme and we
want a UN that truly delivers for
everyone, then at its core, we must
treat every human being as having equal
value and deserving respect.
And I can find no better reference than
his majesty Haley Salassie
speaking in this very assembly on the
4th of October 1963.
And those who know the words can say it
with me. Until the philosophy which
holds one race superior
and another inferior
is finally and permanently
discredited and abandoned.
Everywhere is war.
until
until they are no longer first class and
secondass citizens of any nation.
Until the color of a man's skin has of
no more significance than the color of
his eyes,
there will be war.
But Mr. president equally.
There will be no trust and no
transformation.
We want peace.
And in the words of that iconic song
made famous by Dion Warrick, what the
world needs now is love. Sweet love.
It's the only thing that there's just
too little love. No, not just for some,
but for everyone, love and a little
kindness. So, Mr. President, I end this
statement by returning to the beginning
of a milestones of profound importance
to my country and its relationship to
the world.
The 9th of December this year will mark
60 years since Barbados took its place
in this organization,
emerging into independence
after 340 years of imperial subjugation.
On a wintry 9th of December 1966,
just nine days after we achieved
independence and on the very day of our
admission to the United Nations, our
first prime minister, the right
excellent Errol Barrow, set out what
coupled with the principles of this
organization
has remained our guiding principle in
dealing with the world that Barbados is
a friend of all and a satellite of none.
Indeed, Prime Minister Barrow spoke of a
world marked by profound inequalities in
wealth and opportunity which Fannon had
highlighted only five years earlier in
the text I quoted. And drawing from
Prime Minister Barrow's language where
he quoted from the Hebrew Bible, he
warned that newly independent countries
could not remain heers of wood and
drawers of water while the wealth of the
world flowed elsewhere.
He saw the United Nations as having to
put the eradication of poverty at the
center of its role. Do not question,
therefore, why we view it as our duty to
fight increasing global inequality.
Much good has been done by this UN in
the last 60 and in fact 80 years. During
this time, our membership in the United
Nations has been essential to Barbados's
expression of its sovereignty and its
participation as an equal member of the
international community.
These halls have given us a place to
speak in our own name, to defend the
interests of our people and others, and
to help shape the decisions that affect
us all. Mr. president. Earlier this
year, our poet laurate stood at this
rostrm and reminded us in this assembly
and I quote, "The very name United
Nations implies a commitment to ignite
the fires of conscience, empathy, unity,
and equity.
This UN,
this United Nations must continue to
stoke those fires for a transformed and
inclusive world. I say to you as I leave
this rostroom, let us together ensure
that the flames of hope, peace, and
dignity burn so bright that in the midst
of all the odds against us that they
shine on all of the world. I thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the Prime Minister, Minister for
Economic Affairs and Development and
Minister for National Security of of
Barbados.
